summary.text: The discriminant is a polynomial function of a polynomial's coefficients, and in the quadratic formula it sits under the square root.
It is zero when the polynomial has a repeated root, and with real coefficients it is positive when all the roots are real and simple.
James Joseph Sylvester coined the term in 1851, and discriminants are used in factorization, number theory and algebraic geometry.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The discriminant of a polynomial is an expression built from its coefficients that tells you about the roots without working them out. Once the coefficients are fixed, the discriminant is a single fixed value: unlike the polynomial, it does not change as x changes. More generally, the discriminant is itself a polynomial function of the coefficients.

paragraphs.heading: The quadratic case
paragraphs.text: For a quadratic, the discriminant Δ is the quantity sitting under the square root in the quadratic formula. If Δ = 0, there is just one distinct real root; it is called a double or repeated root, since the two roots are the same, and the parabola touches the x-axis at its vertex. If Δ < 0, there are no real roots and the parabola never meets the x-axis; the two roots are non-real complex conjugates instead. For example, x² − 4 x + 4 = (x − 2)² has Δ = 0 and a repeated root at x = 2.

paragraphs.heading: Why the sign matters
paragraphs.text: The parabola's vertex is at (−b/(2 a), −Δ/(4 a)). That shows in pictures why the sign of the discriminant decides whether the curve crosses, touches or misses the x-axis. Calling the roots r₁ and r₂, another way to write it is Δ = a² (r₁ − r₂)². And when the coefficients are rational numbers, both roots are rational exactly when the discriminant is the square of a rational number.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond quadratics
paragraphs.text: If any polynomial has a multiple root, its discriminant is zero. With real coefficients, the sign was chosen historically so that the discriminant is positive when all the roots are real and distinct. For a cubic with real coefficients, a positive discriminant means three distinct real roots, and a negative one means one real root plus two non-real complex conjugate roots. For higher degrees, the sign alone usually says less about how many real roots there are.

paragraphs.heading: Growing fast
paragraphs.text: For small degrees the discriminant is fairly simple, but for higher ones it can become unwieldy. The discriminant of a general quartic has 16 terms, a quintic's has 59, and a sextic's has 246. At the low end, the discriminant of a linear polynomial is rarely looked at and, when needed, is usually set equal to 1. For a constant polynomial there is no common convention at all.

paragraphs.heading: Name and uses
paragraphs.text: The British mathematician James Joseph Sylvester introduced the term in 1851. Discriminants are put to work in polynomial factorization, number theory and algebraic geometry. Related ideas include the discriminant of an algebraic number field and the discriminant of a quadratic form.
